decks.title: Definite Integrals — Part 1: Evaluation, substitution and basic properties
goals: Evaluate definite integrals with the fundamental theorem of calculus (stated without proof)
Change the limits when using a substitution
Use the dummy-variable, reversal and splitting properties
Integrate modulus and greatest-integer functions by splitting the interval

slides.heading: Definite Integrals, Part 1
slides.body_md: An indefinite integral is a family of functions; a definite integral is a single number.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: find an antiderivative, apply the fundamental theorem, substitute with new limits, use the basic properties, and split modulus and greatest-integer integrands.
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance.

slides.narration: Welcome to definite integrals. You already know how to find antiderivatives. Now we attach limits and get a single number. In this part we learn how to evaluate such integrals, how to handle limits in a substitution, and how to split an interval when the integrand has a corner or a jump.

slides.heading: What you will learn

visual.alt: Table of the three steps of the fundamental theorem: find an antiderivative F of f, write F in square brackets with limits a and b, and subtract F of a from F of b.
visual.caption: The constant $C$ cancels in $F(b) - F(a)$.

slides.narration: Here are the goals. You will use the fundamental theorem to evaluate definite integrals, change the limits in a substitution, use three basic properties, and integrate functions with a modulus or a greatest integer sign by splitting the interval at the right places.

slides.heading: The fundamental theorem of calculus
slides.body_md: If $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$ and $F' = f$, then $\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = F(b) - F(a)$. (The proof is not in the ISC syllabus.)

visual.alt: Table of the three steps of the fundamental theorem: find an antiderivative F of f, write F in square brackets with limits a and b, and subtract F of a from F of b.
visual.caption: The constant $C$ cancels in $F(b) - F(a)$.

slides.narration: The fundamental theorem links definite integrals with antiderivatives. If F is any antiderivative of a continuous function f, the integral from a to b is F at b minus F at a. The constant of integration cancels, so it is never written. We use this theorem without proof.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: direct evaluation
slides.body_md: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_1^2 \left(3x^2 - \dfrac{1}{x^2}\right)dx$.

visual.alt: Worked example table: the antiderivative of 3 x squared minus 1 over x squared is x cubed plus 1 over x; at 2 it is 17 over 2, at 1 it is 2, so the integral from 1 to 2 is 13 over 2.
visual.caption: Checked by quadrature.

slides.narration: First find an antiderivative: x cubed plus one over x. Substitute the upper limit two to get seventeen halves, and the lower limit one to get two. Subtract to obtain thirteen halves. Write the bracket with its limits; it earns a method mark in the examination.

slides.heading: Signed area
slides.body_md: Where the curve is below the axis, the integral counts the area as negative.

visual.alt: Graph of y equals x squared minus 2 x on minus 0.5 to 3. The curve crosses the x axis at 0 and at 2, dips below the axis between them, and rises to 3 at x equals 3.
visual.caption: Below the axis the integrand is negative: $\int_0^2 (x^2 - 2x)\,dx = -\tfrac43$.

slides.narration: A definite integral adds up the integrand along the interval. Where the curve lies below the axis, the contribution is negative. For x squared minus two x between zero and two, the whole curve is below the axis, so the integral is minus four thirds, even though the area itself is positive.

slides.heading: Quick check: new limits
slides.body_md: Choose the correct new limits after a substitution.
slides.narration: Put the old limits into the formula for t. What values of t do you get?

slides.heading: Substitution with new limits
slides.body_md: If $t = g(x)$, then $\displaystyle\int_a^b f(g(x))g'(x)\,dx = \int_{g(a)}^{g(b)} f(t)\,dt$.

visual.alt: Table of two substitutions with changed limits: e to the sin x times cos x from 0 to pi by 2 becomes the integral of e to the t from 0 to 1, which is e minus 1; and 2 x times x squared minus 1 squared from 1 to 2 becomes the integral of t squared from 0 to 3, which is 9.
visual.caption: Change the limits and stay in $t$.

slides.narration: When you substitute in a definite integral, change the limits too. The new limits are the values of t at the old limits. Then you can finish entirely in t, without returning to x. The table shows two examples, one with an exponential and one with a power of a bracket.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a substitution
slides.body_md: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} e^{\sin x}\cos x\,dx$.

visual.alt: Table of two substitutions with changed limits: e to the sin x times cos x from 0 to pi by 2 becomes the integral of e to the t from 0 to 1, which is e minus 1; and 2 x times x squared minus 1 squared from 1 to 2 becomes the integral of t squared from 0 to 3, which is 9.
visual.caption: Change the limits and stay in $t$.

slides.narration: The derivative of sine x is present, so put t equal to sine x. When x is zero, t is zero; when x is a right angle, t is one. The integral becomes the integral of e to the t from zero to one, which is e minus one.

slides.heading: Three basic properties
slides.body_md: Rename the variable, reverse the limits, split the interval.

visual.alt: Table of the three basic properties: the variable can be renamed, reversing the limits changes the sign, and the interval can be split at any point c.
visual.caption: Splitting is the key to modulus and greatest-integer integrands.

slides.narration: Three simple properties are used all the time. The letter used for the variable does not matter. Reversing the limits changes the sign, so an integral from a to a is zero. And the interval may be split at any point c, which is the key to integrands with corners or jumps.

slides.heading: Quick check: a missing limit
slides.body_md: Find the upper limit that gives a stated value.
slides.narration: Evaluate the integral in terms of k, then solve.

slides.heading: Integrating a modulus
slides.body_md: Split where the expression inside the modulus changes sign.

visual.alt: Graph of y equals the modulus of x minus 1 on 0 to 3: a V shape with its corner on the x axis at x equals 1, rising to 1 at x equals 0 and to 2 at x equals 3.
visual.caption: Two triangles: areas $\tfrac12$ and $2$, total $\tfrac52$.

slides.narration: A modulus function has a corner where the inside is zero. For the modulus of x minus one, the corner is at one. On each side, the modulus is a simple linear function, so split the interval at one and integrate the two pieces separately. Here the pieces are two triangles.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a modulus with two sign changes
slides.body_md: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{2} |x^2 - x|\,dx$.
bullets: $x^2 - x = x(x - 1)$ changes sign at $0$ and $1$

visual.alt: Worked example table for the integral of the modulus of x squared minus x from minus 1 to 2: split at 0 and 1; the pieces are 5 over 6, 1 over 6 and 5 over 6, adding to 11 over 6.
visual.caption: Total $\dfrac{11}{6}$.

slides.narration: Factorise the expression inside: x times x minus one. It changes sign at zero and at one, so split the interval there. Between zero and one the expression is negative, so we integrate its negative. Adding the three pieces gives eleven sixths.

slides.heading: The greatest integer function
slides.body_md: Split at every integer inside the interval: on each piece $[x]$ is a constant.

visual.alt: Graph of the greatest integer function on 0 to 2.5 as three flat steps: height 0 on 0 to 1, height 1 on 1 to 2, and height 2 on 2 to 2.5, each step closed at its left end.
visual.caption: Steps of width $1$, $1$ and $0.5$: $\int_0^{2.5}[x]\,dx = 0 + 1 + 1 = 2$.

slides.narration: The greatest integer function is a staircase. On each step it is constant, so integrating it means adding the areas of rectangles. Split the interval at every integer it contains. Here the steps have heights zero, one and two, and the last step is only half a unit wide.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a shifted staircase
slides.body_md: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^2 \left[x + \tfrac12\right]dx$.
bullets: Jumps where $x + \dfrac12$ is a whole number: $x = \dfrac12$ and $x = \dfrac32$

visual.alt: Worked example table for the greatest integer of x plus one half from 0 to 2: it is 0 up to one half, 1 from one half to three halves, and 2 from three halves to 2; the contributions 0, 1 and 1 add to 2.
visual.caption: Jumps occur where $x + \tfrac12$ is a whole number.

slides.narration: The jumps happen where x plus one half is a whole number, at one half and at three halves. On the three pieces the function takes the values zero, one and two. Multiply each value by the width of its piece and add: the integral is two.

slides.heading: Quick check: a staircase integral
slides.body_md: Integrate the greatest integer function over an interval that starts at 1.
slides.narration: List the steps between one and three and a half, with their heights and widths.

slides.heading: Quick check: renaming the variable
slides.body_md: Find the value of an integral written with the letter t.
slides.narration: Does the name of the variable change the number?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: $\displaystyle\int_a^b f = F(b) - F(a)$ (theorem used without proof)
Modulus and $[x]$: split at sign changes and jumps

nodes.label: Modulus and $[x]$: split at sign changes and jumps

visual.alt: Summary flow for Part 1: evaluate as F of b minus F of a, change the limits when substituting, use reversal, renaming and splitting, and split modulus and greatest-integer integrands at sign changes and jumps.
visual.caption: Part 1 in one line.

slides.narration: To sum up. A definite integral is F at b minus F at a. In a substitution, change the limits and finish in the new variable. Reversing the limits changes the sign, the variable can be renamed, and the interval can be split. Split modulus and greatest integer integrands where they change.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Change the limits when you substitute
Mark every split point on a number line
Check the sign of each piece of a modulus

rows: correct split points 1, signs or step values 1, total 1
keeping the old limits after substituting

visual.alt: Exam tips table for Part 1: direct evaluation earns marks for the antiderivative and the substituted limits; substitution earns marks for t and dt, the new limits and the value; modulus and greatest-integer questions earn marks for the split points, the signs or steps, and the total; the common slip is keeping the old limits.
visual.caption: Show every split point clearly.

slides.narration: In the examination, write the antiderivative in a bracket with its limits. When you substitute, change the limits; keeping the old limits is the most common slip. For a modulus or a greatest integer function, mark the split points on a number line before you integrate, and check the sign on each piece.

decks.title: Definite Integrals — Part 2: Reflection, symmetry, even and odd functions
goals: Prove and use the a + b − x and a − x properties
Evaluate integrals of the form x f(sin x) over [0, π]
Use the [0, 2a] property for symmetric and antisymmetric integrands
Use even and odd functions on balanced intervals

slides.heading: Definite Integrals, Part 2
slides.body_md: Some integrals that have no easy antiderivative can still be evaluated exactly by symmetry.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: the reflection a plus b minus x, its special case a minus x, the property over 0 to 2 a, and even and odd functions on minus a to a.
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. Here we meet properties that come from reflecting the interval. They let us evaluate integrals whose antiderivatives are hard or impossible to write down. Each property is proved with a single substitution, and each has a typical kind of question.

slides.heading: What you will learn
bullets: Even and odd functions on $[-a, a]$

rows: limits that add up to the number inside

visual.alt: Table of the reflection properties: P3 replaces x by a plus b minus x; P4 replaces x by a minus x on 0 to a; P5 splits 0 to 2 a at a; P6 doubles an even function and kills an odd one on minus a to a.
visual.caption: Each is proved by one substitution.

slides.narration: Here are the goals. You will learn the reflection property and its special case on an interval starting at zero, the property over an interval from zero to two a, and the rules for even and odd functions on a balanced interval.

slides.heading: Reflecting the interval
slides.body_md: $\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = \int_a^b f(a + b - x)\,dx$

visual.alt: Graph on 1 to 4 of y equals x squared over 4 plus 1 and its mirror image y equals 5 minus x all squared over 4 plus 1. The two curves are reflections of each other in the line x equals 2.5, so they enclose equal areas over 1 to 4.
visual.caption: Reflecting in $x = \tfrac{a + b}{2}$ does not change the integral.

slides.narration: Replacing x by a plus b minus x reflects the graph in the middle of the interval. A reflection does not change the area, so the integral is unchanged. The proof is one substitution: put t equal to a plus b minus x, and the limits swap while d x becomes minus d t.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: reflect and add
slides.body_md: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_1^3 \dfrac{\sqrt[3]{x}}{\sqrt[3]{x} + \sqrt[3]{4 - x}}\,dx$.
bullets: The reflected form swaps the two cube roots

visual.alt: Worked example table: call the integral of the cube root of x over the sum of the cube roots of x and 4 minus x from 1 to 3 I; reflecting with a plus b equal to 4 swaps the roots; adding gives 2 I equals 2, so I equals 1.
visual.caption: Checked by quadrature.

slides.narration: The limits one and three add up to four, the same four that appears inside the root. That is the signal to reflect. The reflected integral has the two cube roots swapped. Adding the original and the reflected form, the numerators add up to the denominator, so twice I is the length of the interval.

slides.heading: Quick check: the reflection property
slides.body_md: Choose the correct form of the property on an interval starting at zero.
slides.narration: Think of the substitution t equals a minus x. What happens to the limits?

slides.heading: The factor x and the property
slides.body_md: $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi} x f(\sin x)\,dx = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\int_0^{\pi} f(\sin x)\,dx$

rows: limits that add up to the number inside

visual.alt: Table of the reflection properties: P3 replaces x by a plus b minus x; P4 replaces x by a minus x on 0 to a; P5 splits 0 to 2 a at a; P6 doubles an even function and kills an odd one on minus a to a.
visual.caption: Each is proved by one substitution.

slides.narration: A factor x in the integrand is awkward, but reflection removes it. Since sine of pi minus x is sine x, reflecting turns x into pi minus x and leaves the rest unchanged. Adding the two forms gives pi times the integral without the x, so the original is half of that.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: the factor x disappears
slides.body_md: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi} x\sin^4 x\,dx$.

visual.alt: Worked example table for the integral of x times sin to the fourth x from 0 to pi: use the x times f of sin x property, find the integral of sin to the fourth x over 0 to pi as 3 pi by 8, and multiply by pi by 2 to get 3 pi squared by 16.
visual.caption: The factor $x$ disappears after reflecting.

slides.narration: Here f of sine x is sine to the fourth power. By the property, the integral is pi by two times the integral of sine to the fourth over zero to pi. Reducing the fourth power with the double angle identity gives three pi by eight. Multiplying, the value is three pi squared by sixteen.

slides.heading: Quick check: reflect and add
slides.body_md: Find the value of a root quotient whose limits add up to ten.
slides.narration: Reflect, add the two forms, and divide the length of the interval by two.

slides.heading: Odd functions on a balanced interval
slides.body_md: If $f(-x) = -f(x)$, then $\displaystyle\int_{-a}^{a} f(x)\,dx = 0$.

visual.alt: Graph of the odd function y equals x cubed minus 2 x on minus 1.8 to 1.8. The part on the left is the part on the right turned through half a turn about the origin, so areas above and below the axis cancel over a balanced interval.
visual.caption: Odd: $f(-x) = -f(x)$, so $\int_{-a}^{a} f = 0$.

slides.narration: An odd function satisfies f of minus x equals minus f of x. Its graph is unchanged by a half turn about the origin, so the part above the axis on one side is matched by an equal part below the axis on the other. Over a balanced interval the integral is zero.

slides.heading: Even functions on a balanced interval
slides.body_md: If $f(-x) = f(x)$, then $\displaystyle\int_{-a}^{a} f(x)\,dx = 2\int_0^a f(x)\,dx$.

visual.alt: Graph of the even function y equals cos x plus x squared over 4 on minus 2 to 2. It is a mirror image of itself in the y axis, so the area on minus a to 0 equals the area on 0 to a.
visual.caption: Even: $f(-x) = f(x)$, so $\int_{-a}^{a} f = 2\int_0^a f$.

slides.narration: An even function satisfies f of minus x equals f of x, so its graph is a mirror image in the vertical axis. The integral over the left half equals the integral over the right half, so the whole is twice the integral from zero to a.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: even and odd parts
slides.body_md: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1} \left(e^x - e^{-x} + 3x^2\right)dx$.

visual.alt: Worked example table for the integral of e to the x minus e to the minus x plus 3 x squared from minus 1 to 1: the exponential part is odd and contributes 0; 3 x squared is even and contributes 2; the value is 2.
visual.caption: Value $2$.

slides.narration: Split the integrand into parts and test each one. Replacing x by minus x turns e to the x minus e to the minus x into its negative, so that part is odd and contributes nothing. Three x squared is even, so its integral is twice the integral from zero to one, which is two.

slides.heading: Quick check: an even and an odd part
slides.body_md: Integrate a sum of an even power and an odd term over minus one to one.
slides.narration: Which term is odd and vanishes? Double the integral of the other from zero to one.

slides.heading: The property over [0, 2a]
slides.body_md: $\displaystyle\int_0^{2a} f = 2\int_0^a f$ if $f(2a - x) = f(x)$, and $0$ if $f(2a - x) = -f(x)$.

visual.alt: Graph of y equals sin cubed x on 0 to about 6.3. The hump above the axis on 0 to pi is matched by an equal hump below the axis on pi to 2 pi.
visual.caption: Since $\sin^3(2\pi - x) = -\sin^3 x$, $\int_0^{2\pi} \sin^3 x\,dx = 0$.

slides.narration: Over an interval from zero to two a, compare f at two a minus x with f at x. If they are equal, the graph is symmetric about a, and the integral is twice the integral over the first half. If one is the negative of the other, the halves cancel and the integral is zero, like sine cubed over a full turn.

slides.heading: Worked example 8: twice the half
slides.body_md: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi} |\cos x|\,dx$.

rows: $|\cos(\pi - x)| = |\cos x|$, so use P5 with $a = \tfrac{\pi}{2}$

visual.alt: Worked example table for the integral of the modulus of cos x from 0 to pi: the integrand is symmetric about pi by 2, so the integral is twice the integral of cos x from 0 to pi by 2, which gives 2.
visual.caption: No splitting by sign is needed.

slides.narration: The modulus of cosine is symmetric about a right angle, because cosine of pi minus x is minus cosine x and the modulus removes the sign. So the integral is twice the integral over the first half, where cosine is positive. That gives two, without splitting by sign.

slides.heading: Quick check: true or false?
slides.body_md: Decide whether doubling the half works for every function on a balanced interval.
slides.narration: Test the rule on the simplest odd function you know.

slides.heading: Which property?
slides.body_md: Look at the limits before you integrate.

nodes.label: Do the limits add to a number inside the integrand?
Use P3 or P4 and add the two forms
Split into even and odd parts (P6)
Use P5: twice the half, or zero

visual.alt: Decision flow for choosing a property: if the limits add up to a number inside the integrand, reflect and add; if the interval is balanced, split into even and odd parts; if it is 0 to 2 a with symmetry about a, double the half or get zero.
visual.caption: Which property? Look at the limits first.

slides.narration: When a definite integral looks hard, look at the limits first. If they add up to a number inside the integrand, reflect and add. If the interval is balanced, split into even and odd parts. If it runs from zero to two a, test the symmetry about a.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Reflect $x \to a + b - x$ and add the two forms
$[0, 2a]$: double the half or get zero

visual.alt: Summary flow for Part 2: reflect and add the two forms; for x times f of sin x take out pi by 2; over 0 to 2 a double the half or get zero; over a balanced interval an odd function gives 0 and an even one doubles.
visual.caption: Part 2 in one line.

slides.narration: To sum up. Reflection does not change a definite integral, and adding the original and reflected forms often gives a simple integrand. A factor x with a function of sine x is removed by reflection. Over zero to two a, test the symmetry about a. On a balanced interval, odd parts vanish and even parts double.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: State the property you use by name
In a proof, show the substitution and the new limits

rows: test $f(-x)$ 1, use of the property 1, value 1
parts such as 2 + 3: a proof, then an application

visual.alt: Exam tips table for Part 2: a property proof earns marks for the substitution and the conclusion; reflect-and-add earns marks for the reflected form, the sum and the value; even and odd questions earn marks for testing f of minus x and using the property; long questions combine a proof and an application.
visual.caption: Name the property you use.

slides.narration: In the examination, name the property you are using. In a proof, show the substitution, the new limits and the change of sign from d x. When you claim a function is even or odd, show the test. And when you reflect and add, write two I equals the new integral before dividing by two.

notes.title: Definite Integrals — chapter notes

sections.heading: 1. The fundamental theorem of calculus
sections.body_md:
If $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$ and $F$ is any antiderivative of $f$, then $\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = F(b) - F(a)$. The theorem is used **without proof** (its proof is not in the ISC 2027 syllabus).

- The constant of integration cancels, so it is never written.
- The integral counts area below the axis as negative.
- The theorem needs $f$ continuous on the **closed** interval: $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1} \dfrac{dx}{x^2}$ cannot be found this way.

key_terms.definition_md: The number $\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$, equal to $F(b) - F(a)$ for continuous $f$.

visual.alt: Table of the three steps of the fundamental theorem: find an antiderivative F of f, write F in square brackets with limits a and b, and subtract F of a from F of b.
visual.caption: The constant $C$ cancels in $F(b) - F(a)$.

visuals.alt: Worked example table: the antiderivative of 3 x squared minus 1 over x squared is x cubed plus 1 over x; at 2 it is 17 over 2, at 1 it is 2, so the integral from 1 to 2 is 13 over 2.
visuals.caption: Checked by quadrature.

visuals.alt: Graph of y equals x squared minus 2 x on minus 0.5 to 3. The curve crosses the x axis at 0 and at 2, dips below the axis between them, and rises to 3 at x equals 3.
visuals.caption: Below the axis the integrand is negative: $\int_0^2 (x^2 - 2x)\,dx = -\tfrac43$.

sections.heading: 2. Substitution with changed limits
sections.body_md:
If $t = g(x)$, then $\displaystyle\int_a^b f(g(x))g'(x)\,dx = \int_{g(a)}^{g(b)} f(t)\,dt$.

Find the new limits by putting the old limits into $t = g(x)$, then finish in $t$. Do not return to $x$, and do not keep the old limits.

key_terms.definition_md: The values of t at the old limits.

visual.alt: Table of two substitutions with changed limits: e to the sin x times cos x from 0 to pi by 2 becomes the integral of e to the t from 0 to 1, which is e minus 1; and 2 x times x squared minus 1 squared from 1 to 2 becomes the integral of t squared from 0 to 3, which is 9.
visual.caption: Change the limits and stay in $t$.

sections.heading: 3. Basic properties; modulus and greatest-integer integrands
sections.body_md:
- **P0** $\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = \int_a^b f(t)\,dt$ (dummy variable)
- **P1** $\displaystyle\int_a^b f = -\int_b^a f$; in particular $\displaystyle\int_a^a f = 0$
- **P2** $\displaystyle\int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f$

**Modulus:** split where the inside changes sign and remove the modulus on each piece with the correct sign.

**Greatest integer $[x]$:** split at every integer (or every point where the inside is an integer); on each piece the function is constant.

key_terms.definition_md: A point where the integrand changes formula: a zero inside a modulus or a jump of [x].

visual.alt: Table of the three basic properties: the variable can be renamed, reversing the limits changes the sign, and the interval can be split at any point c.
visual.caption: Splitting is the key to modulus and greatest-integer integrands.

visuals.alt: Graph of y equals the modulus of x minus 1 on 0 to 3: a V shape with its corner on the x axis at x equals 1, rising to 1 at x equals 0 and to 2 at x equals 3.
visuals.caption: Two triangles: areas $\tfrac12$ and $2$, total $\tfrac52$.

visuals.alt: Worked example table for the integral of the modulus of x squared minus x from minus 1 to 2: split at 0 and 1; the pieces are 5 over 6, 1 over 6 and 5 over 6, adding to 11 over 6.
visuals.caption: Total $\dfrac{11}{6}$.

visuals.alt: Graph of the greatest integer function on 0 to 2.5 as three flat steps: height 0 on 0 to 1, height 1 on 1 to 2, and height 2 on 2 to 2.5, each step closed at its left end.
visuals.caption: Steps of width $1$, $1$ and $0.5$: $\int_0^{2.5}[x]\,dx = 0 + 1 + 1 = 2$.

visuals.alt: Worked example table for the greatest integer of x plus one half from 0 to 2: it is 0 up to one half, 1 from one half to three halves, and 2 from three halves to 2; the contributions 0, 1 and 1 add to 2.
visuals.caption: Jumps occur where $x + \tfrac12$ is a whole number.

sections.heading: 4. Reflection: the a + b − x and a − x properties
sections.body_md:
- **P3** $\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = \int_a^b f(a + b - x)\,dx$
- **P4** $\displaystyle\int_0^a f(x)\,dx = \int_0^a f(a - x)\,dx$

**Proof (P4):** put $t = a - x$; then $dx = -dt$, $x = 0 \Rightarrow t = a$, $x = a \Rightarrow t = 0$, so the integral becomes $-\displaystyle\int_a^0 f(t)\,dt = \int_0^a f(t)\,dt$.

**Reflect and add:** call the integral $I$, write the reflected form, add the two, and divide by $2$. On $\left[0, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$, P4 swaps $\sin x$ and $\cos x$; it also shows $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} \log\tan x\,dx = 0$.

**The factor $x$:** $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi} x f(\sin x)\,dx = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\int_0^{\pi} f(\sin x)\,dx$.

key_terms.definition_md: Replacing x by a + b − x, which mirrors the graph in the middle of the interval.

visual.alt: Graph on 1 to 4 of y equals x squared over 4 plus 1 and its mirror image y equals 5 minus x all squared over 4 plus 1. The two curves are reflections of each other in the line x equals 2.5, so they enclose equal areas over 1 to 4.
visual.caption: Reflecting in $x = \tfrac{a + b}{2}$ does not change the integral.

rows: limits that add up to the number inside

visuals.alt: Table of the reflection properties: P3 replaces x by a plus b minus x; P4 replaces x by a minus x on 0 to a; P5 splits 0 to 2 a at a; P6 doubles an even function and kills an odd one on minus a to a.
visuals.caption: Each is proved by one substitution.

sections.heading: 5. The [0, 2a] property
sections.body_md:
- **P5** $\displaystyle\int_0^{2a} f(x)\,dx = \int_0^a f(x)\,dx + \int_0^a f(2a - x)\,dx$

So $\displaystyle\int_0^{2a} f = 2\int_0^a f$ if $f(2a - x) = f(x)$, and $\displaystyle\int_0^{2a} f = 0$ if $f(2a - x) = -f(x)$.

Examples: $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi} \sin^5 x\,dx = 2\int_0^{\pi/2} \sin^5 x\,dx$; $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi} \cos^3 x\,dx = 0$; $\displaystyle\int_0^{2\pi} \sin^3 x\,dx = 0$.

sections.heading: 6. Even and odd functions on [−a, a]
sections.body_md:
- **Even:** $f(-x) = f(x)$, e.g. $x^2$, $\cos x$, $|x|$; then $\displaystyle\int_{-a}^{a} f = 2\int_0^a f$.
- **Odd:** $f(-x) = -f(x)$, e.g. $x^3$, $\sin x$, $x\cos x$, $\log\dfrac{2 - x}{2 + x}$; then $\displaystyle\int_{-a}^{a} f = 0$.

Any integrand can be split into an even part and an odd part; integrate only the even part. The interval must be balanced: on $[-1, 2]$ these rules do not apply.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How ISC marks are awarded**
- *Direct evaluation (1–2 marks):* antiderivative, then limits substituted and simplified.
- *Substitution (2–3 marks):* $t$ and $dt$, the new limits, the value.
- *Modulus or greatest integer (2–3 marks):* split points, signs or step values, total.
- *Property proofs (2 marks):* the substitution with changed limits and the conclusion.
- *Section D (5 marks):* often a proof in part (a) and an application in part (b).

**Common mistakes**
- Keeping the old limits after a substitution.
- Forgetting to change the sign of a modulus on the piece where the inside is negative.
- Using the even-function rule on an interval that is not balanced.
- Applying the fundamental theorem when the integrand blows up inside the interval.

questions.solution_md: When $x = 0$, $t = 1$; when $x = 2$, $t = 5$. The integral becomes $\dfrac12\displaystyle\int_1^5 \dfrac{dt}{t} = \dfrac12\log 5$. Keeping the old limits (option b) is the usual slip.

questions.solution_md: $\displaystyle\int_1^4 f(x)\,dx = F(4) - F(1) = 10 - 3 = 7$. The theorem is used without proof in the ISC syllabus.

questions.stem_md: For a function $f$ with $\displaystyle\int_0^3 f(x)\,dx = 10$ and $\displaystyle\int_0^1 f(x)\,dx = 4$, splitting the interval at $1$ gives $\displaystyle\int_1^3 f(x)\,dx =$

Because the letter used for the variable does not matter, $\displaystyle\int_0^2 t^3\,dt$ has the same value as $\displaystyle\int_0^2 x^3\,dx$. That common value is

Therefore $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1} g(x)\,dx = 0$.

(b) It is known that $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} \log(\sin x)\,dx = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}\log 2$. Using part (a), evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} \log(3\sin x\cos x)\,dx$. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Put $t = a - x$, $dt = -dx$; $x = 0 \Rightarrow t = a$, $x = a \Rightarrow t = 0$. So $\displaystyle\int_0^a f(a - x)\,dx = -\int_a^0 f(t)\,dt = \int_0^a f(t)\,dt = \int_0^a f(x)\,dx$.

**(b)** $\log(3\sin x\cos x) = \log 3 + \log\sin x + \log\cos x$. By (a), $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} \log\cos x\,dx = \int_0^{\pi/2} \log\sin x\,dx = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}\log 2$.

questions.stem_md:

(b) Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1} \dfrac{x^3 + |x| + 1}{x^2 + 2|x| + 1}\,dx$. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $\displaystyle\int_{-a}^{a} f = \int_{-a}^{0} f + \int_0^a f$. In the first, put $x = -t$: $\displaystyle\int_{-a}^0 f(x)\,dx = \int_0^a f(-t)\,dt = \int_0^a f(t)\,dt$ for even $f$. Hence the result.

**(b)** The denominator is $(|x| + 1)^2$, which is even. The part $\dfrac{x^3}{(|x| + 1)^2}$ is odd and contributes $0$. The rest is $\dfrac{|x| + 1}{(|x| + 1)^2} = \dfrac{1}{|x| + 1}$, which is even.

Value $= 2\displaystyle\int_0^1 \dfrac{dx}{1 + x} = 2\log 2$.

(b) Hence evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi} x\cos^2 x\,dx$, writing $\cos^2 x$ as a function of $\sin x$. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $I = \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi} (\pi - x) f(\sin(\pi - x))\,dx = \int_0^{\pi} (\pi - x) f(\sin x)\,dx = \pi\int_0^{\pi} f(\sin x)\,dx - I$, so $I = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi} f(\sin x)\,dx$.

(b) Hence, with $t = \cos x$ for the last step, evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi} \sin^5 x\,dx$. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $\displaystyle\int_0^{2a} f = \int_0^a f + \int_a^{2a} f$. In the second, put $x = 2a - t$: $\displaystyle\int_a^{2a} f(x)\,dx = \int_0^a f(2a - t)\,dt$.

**(b)** With $a = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, $\sin^5(\pi - x) = \sin^5 x$, so the integral is $2\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} \sin^5 x\,dx$.

With $t = \cos x$: $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} \sin^5 x\,dx = \int_0^1 (1 - t^2)^2\,dt = 1 - \dfrac23 + \dfrac15 = \dfrac{8}{15}$.

Value $= \dfrac{16}{15}$.
